subject: physics

items.q: Which statement correctly describes the molecules of a gas and what the temperature of the gas tells you?
items.correct: They are in constant random motion, and the temperature is related to their average kinetic energy.
items.misconception: They all travel at one fixed speed, and the temperature is related to that single shared speed.
items.why: Textbook animations often show identical particles moving at identical speeds, and 'random' is read as meaning random direction only. The motion is random in both direction and speed. Collisions constantly speed some molecules up and slow others down, so at any instant there is a spread of speeds. That is exactly why the specification speaks of the average kinetic energy.
items.random_wrong: They are in constant random motion, and the temperature is related to the total kinetic energy of the gas.

items.q: A sealed metal can holds a gas. The can is rigid, so the volume of the gas cannot change. The can is warmed gently. Why does the pressure of the gas rise?
items.correct: The molecules gain kinetic energy, so they strike the walls harder and more often each second.
items.misconception: The molecules themselves swell as they warm, so they press more tightly on the walls.
items.why: Students meet thermal expansion of solids and liquids first and carry 'heating makes things bigger' down to the particle scale. Diagrams that draw hot gas particles as larger circles reinforce it. Heating changes how fast the molecules move, not how big they are. The size of a molecule does not change with temperature. It is the greater average kinetic energy — faster molecules, more frequent and harder collisions — that raises the pressure.
items.random_wrong: The molecules strike the walls harder, but the number of strikes each second is unchanged.

items.q: What causes the pressure that a gas exerts on the wall of its container?
items.correct: Molecules colliding with the wall, each collision exerting a small force on the wall.
items.misconception: The weight of the gas pressing down on the wall, because gravity pulls the gas downwards.
items.why: The word 'pressure' is met first with solids resting on surfaces and with the weight of liquid columns, where the force really is the weight acting downwards. Gas pressure comes from molecular collisions, which happen on every wall — top, bottom and sides. The net force on each surface is at right angles to that surface, so on a lid above the gas the force pushes upwards.
items.random_wrong: The molecules repelling one another, pushing the outer ones firmly against the wall.

items.q: A fixed mass of gas is sealed in a rigid container, so its volume is constant. Its temperature is lowered. What happens to the pressure of the gas, and why?
items.correct: It falls, because slower molecules hit the walls less often and with less force.
items.misconception: It stays the same, because the volume of the container has not been changed.
items.why: The temperature–pressure link at constant volume is usually taught first and taught hard, so 'temperature causes pressure' becomes the only mechanism students have. There are two separate situations in this section. At constant volume, changing the temperature changes the pressure. At constant temperature, changing the volume changes the pressure, and pressure × volume = constant lets you calculate the new value.
items.random_wrong: It falls, because the cooled molecules shrink and so press less on the walls.

items.q: A flat plate is held inside a container of gas. In which direction does the gas pressure produce a net force on the plate?
items.correct: A net force at right angles to the surface.
items.misconception: A net force straight downwards on the surface.
items.why: The word 'pressure' is met first with solids resting on surfaces and with the weight of liquid columns, where the force really is the weight acting downwards. Gas pressure comes from molecular collisions, which happen on every wall — top, bottom and sides. The net force on each surface is at right angles to that surface, so on a lid above the gas the force pushes upwards.
items.random_wrong: A net force slanted along the surface it strikes.

items.q: A sealed syringe contains a fixed mass of gas. The plunger is pulled out very slowly, so the temperature of the gas stays constant. Using the particle model, why does the pressure of the gas decrease?
items.correct: The molecules spread through a bigger volume, so fewer hit each area of wall per second.
items.misconception: The molecules slow down when given more room, so each strike on the wall is weaker.
items.why: Students correctly link crowding to more collisions, then wrongly assume the collisions themselves must be gentler or fiercer, because that is the only cause of a pressure change they can picture. At constant temperature the average kinetic energy is fixed, so the molecules keep the same average speed. What changes is how far they travel between hits on the walls, and therefore how often each area of wall is struck. Frequency of collisions, not their violence, explains the pressure change.
items.random_wrong: The molecules are further apart, so they collide with one another far less often.

items.q: Under which conditions does pressure × volume = constant apply to a gas?
items.correct: For a fixed mass of gas held at a constant temperature.
items.misconception: For any gas whose temperature is changing but whose mass is fixed.
items.why: The temperature–pressure link at constant volume is usually taught first and taught hard, so 'temperature causes pressure' becomes the only mechanism students have. There are two separate situations in this section. At constant volume, changing the temperature changes the pressure. At constant temperature, changing the volume changes the pressure, and pressure × volume = constant lets you calculate the new value.
items.random_wrong: For a fixed mass of gas held in a container of constant volume.

items.q: A fixed mass of gas is held at a constant temperature. For this gas, p V = 24 (with p in Pa and V in m^3). Which pair of readings is possible for this gas?
items.correct: p = 6 Pa, V = 4 m^3
items.why: 'Stays the same' is read as applying to a total, and adding is the operation students reach for first when two quantities have to balance. The equation is pressure × volume = constant. It is the product, not the sum, that is fixed, so the two quantities change by the same factor rather than by the same amount.

items.q: Which units must be used for pressure and volume in the equation p V = constant?
items.correct: pressure in pascals, volume in metres cubed
items.misconception: pressure in newtons, volume in metres cubed
items.why: Pressure is taught as force spread over area and is described in class as a push, so the force unit sticks to it. Force is measured in newtons; pressure is force per unit area and is measured in pascals. The specification states pressure, p, in pascals, Pa.
items.random_wrong: pressure in pascals, volume in centimetres cubed

items.q: A sealed container holds a gas in a volume of 5000 cm^3. What is this volume in the unit required by the equation p V = constant?
items.why: Students apply a familiar length conversion to a volume without noticing that the factor between the units has to be cubed. 1 m = 100 cm, so 1 m^3 = 100 x 100 x 100 = 1 000 000 cm^3. To convert a volume from cm^3 into the m^3 the specification requires, divide by 1 000 000.

items.q: A fixed mass of gas at a constant temperature has a volume of 0.020 m^3 at a pressure of 150 000 Pa. It is compressed to a volume of 0.005 m^3. What is the new pressure of the gas?
items.why: Almost every relationship met before this one is direct proportion, so students expect 'one goes down, the other goes down' and read 'constant' as meaning the two quantities stay in step. The specification states pressure × volume = constant. Their product is fixed, so when one is halved the other must double. Check every answer against common sense: squashing a gas into a smaller space always raises its pressure.

items.q: A fixed mass of gas at a constant temperature has a volume of 0.60 m^3 at a pressure of 200 000 Pa. The pressure is reduced to 50 000 Pa. What is the new volume of the gas?
items.why: Almost every relationship met before this one is direct proportion, so students expect 'one goes down, the other goes down' and read 'constant' as meaning the two quantities stay in step. The specification states pressure × volume = constant. Their product is fixed, so when one is halved the other must double. Check every answer against common sense: squashing a gas into a smaller space always raises its pressure.

items.q: In physics, what is meant by work?
items.correct: Work is the transfer of energy by a force.
items.misconception: Work is the transfer of energy by heating a gas.
items.why: Both do raise the internal energy of a gas, and both are described loosely as 'giving it energy', so students see no reason to keep the two apart. They are different transfers. Heating transfers energy because of a temperature difference; work transfers energy because a force moves something. A pump warms the gas by doing work on it, with no hotter object involved anywhere.
items.random_wrong: Work is the energy stored inside a squashed gas.

items.q: A gas is squashed quickly inside a sealed, well-insulated container, so no energy is transferred to it by heating. What happens to the gas?
items.correct: Work is done on it, so its internal energy rises and it can get hotter.
items.misconception: Nothing changes its energy, because no energy is transferred by heating.
items.why: Temperature change is introduced through heating and cooling, so heating becomes the only route students accept to a hotter substance. Doing work on a gas increases the internal energy of the gas and can cause an increase in the temperature of the gas. Work is a second route by which energy reaches the gas, and it needs no hotter object at all.
items.random_wrong: Its temperature rises, but the internal energy of the gas stays the same.

items.q: After a tyre has been inflated, the barrel of the bicycle pump is noticeably warm — warmer than the tyre and warmer than the hands holding it. What is the best explanation?
items.correct: The piston does work on the gas, raising its internal energy and temperature.
items.misconception: Friction between the piston and barrel is the only cause of the warming.
items.why: Friction is the standard explanation for anything that warms up when it is moved, and there really is some friction in a pump, so the answer feels safe. Friction plays a small part, but the effect the specification asks about is the work done on the gas itself. The force on the piston moves the gas, transferring energy to it, so its internal energy and temperature rise — the gas becomes hot even in a well-oiled pump.
items.random_wrong: Heat flows into the pump from the tyre and from the hands holding it.

items.q: What is the temperature of a gas related to?
items.correct: The average kinetic energy of the molecules.
items.misconception: Temperature tells you the total kinetic energy of all the molecules added together.
items.why: 'Total' and 'average' both sound like ways of describing the whole gas, and students know that a bigger, hotter object stores more energy, so they fuse the two ideas. The specification is precise: the temperature is related to the average kinetic energy of the molecules. A large tank and a small flask of gas at the same temperature have the same average molecular kinetic energy, but the tank holds far more molecules and so far more energy in total.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In which direction does gas pressure produce a net force on a surface?
items.correct: At right angles to the surface.
items.misconception: The force is in whatever direction the molecules happen to be travelling, so it acts at an angle along the wall.
items.why: Students picture one molecule striking the wall at a slant and generalise from that single impact instead of adding up the effect of enormous numbers of impacts from all directions. Molecules do arrive from every direction, but the sideways parts of their impacts cancel out. The specification states that the pressure produces a net force at right angles to the wall of the gas container (or any surface).
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which units must be used in p V = constant?
items.correct: Pressure, p, in pascals, Pa, and volume, V, in metres cubed, m^3.
items.misconception: It does not matter which volume unit you use, as long as you use the same one on both sides.
items.why: In a two-state calculation the units often do cancel, so students who have only ever seen p1V1 = p2V2 conclude that units never matter and stop converting at all. The specification gives the units: pressure in pascals, Pa, and volume in metres cubed, m^3. Quote the volume in m^3 as the specification requires, converting from cm^3 by dividing by 1 000 000.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A gas at constant volume is heated. How do its collisions with the walls change?
items.correct: The molecules hit the walls both more often each second and with a greater force.
items.misconception: The molecules hit the walls harder, but the number of hits each second stays the same.
items.why: Students remember that faster molecules hit harder and stop there, because the container is the same size so they cannot see why the number of hits would change. Faster molecules cross the container in less time, so they return to the walls more often as well as hitting harder. Both effects raise the pressure, and a full explanation names both.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which collisions produce the pressure a gas exerts on its container?
items.correct: Collisions between the molecules and the walls of the container.
items.misconception: Gas pressure is caused by the molecules bumping into each other.
items.why: Particle diagrams draw molecule-on-molecule collisions prominently, and 'pressure' in everyday speech sounds like crowding and jostling. Molecules do collide with one another, but pressure on a surface is the force from collisions with that surface. Explanations of a pressure change must talk about how often, and how hard, molecules hit the wall.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What happens to the internal energy of a gas when work is done on it?
items.correct: The internal energy of the gas increases, and this can cause its temperature to increase.
items.misconception: Internal energy is just another name for temperature, so saying both increase is saying the same thing twice.
items.why: The two always seem to move together in classroom examples, and a thermometer is the only instrument students ever see pointed at the gas. They are different quantities. Internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of all the molecules; temperature is related to their average kinetic energy. Doing work raises the internal energy, and that is what can raise the temperature.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A sealed rigid can of gas is warmed. What happens to the gas?
items.correct: Its volume cannot change, so its pressure rises instead.
items.misconception: Heating a gas always makes it expand, even when it is sealed inside a rigid can.
items.why: The rule 'heating makes gases expand' is met with balloons and syringes, where the container really can change size, and is then applied to every container. A gas expands on heating only if its container allows it. Held at constant volume, the gas cannot expand, so the faster molecules simply strike the walls more often and harder — and it is the pressure that rises.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is work something a gas contains?
items.correct: No. Work is the transfer of energy by a force; what a gas contains is internal energy.
items.misconception: Work is a type of energy stored inside an object, so a compressed gas holds a lot of work.
items.why: Work is measured in joules like every energy store, so students file it alongside the stores rather than alongside the transfers. Work is a transfer, in the same family as heating, not a store. A compressed gas holds internal energy; work is how energy was transferred to it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where does the energy that warms the gas in a bicycle pump come from?
items.correct: From the person pushing the piston, who does work on the enclosed gas.
items.misconception: Heat flows into the pump from the tyre, or from the warm hands gripping it.
items.why: Students look for a hotter object as the source, because heating is the transfer they know best, and both the tyre and the hands are available candidates. The pump becomes warmer than both the tyre and the hands, so energy cannot be flowing in from them. The force on the piston moves the gas and does work on it, raising its internal energy and its temperature.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
